Q18673023.summary: On a golden ground woven with green vine tendrils, a figure crowned with rays rides upward in a chariot drawn by white horses. Set in the vault of a small family tomb beneath St Peter's, alongside Christian mosaics of Jonah, the Good Shepherd and a fisherman, it is widely read as Christ portrayed as the rising sun, the 'Sun of Righteousness' who conquers death. It is one of the earliest Christian mosaics known.
facts: The tomb was first broken into by workmen in 1574 and then sealed again; it lies in the necropolis explored by the Vatican excavations of 1940–1949.
Neighbouring mosaics in the same tomb show Jonah and the whale, the Good Shepherd and a fisherman, which is why the solar charioteer is interpreted as Christ ('Christus-Sol').
An inscription over the doorway, now lost, recorded that the tomb was built for Julius Tarpeianus and his family.
Q18673023.notes: The identification as Christ is an interpretation, not certain. Dating varies: Wikipedia gives 266 CE in one place and 'third or fourth century' in another; Wikidata gives 300. Given broadly.

cur:catacombs-commodilla-lamb-loaves.summary: In a small lunette a pale lamb stands before a row of baskets of bread and touches them with a rod, the gesture with which Christ is shown multiplying the loaves on contemporary sarcophagi. Here Christ appears in the guise of the Lamb of God, performing the miracle of the loaves – a compact image that unites the sacrifice of Christ with the gift of the Eucharistic bread.
facts: Commons gives its size as only 40 × 28 cm and dates it to the mid-4th century.
The rod (virga) touching the baskets is the standard sign of Christ's miracle-working in 4th-century Roman art, transferred here to the Lamb.
cur:catacombs-commodilla-lamb-loaves.notes: The Lamb is a symbolic image of Christ; the identification of the scene with the multiplication of the loaves rests on the iconography.

cur:catacombs-via-salaria-sarcophagus.summary: Between ram-headed ends, a seated philosopher reading and a praying woman flank a central shepherd carrying a sheep, with other figures in a tranquil landscape. The sarcophagus speaks Christian hope in a language its pagan neighbours would have recognised: the Good Shepherd stands at the centre between learning and prayer.
facts: It is dated by the Museo Pio Cristiano to about 250–275 (inv. 31540), before the Peace of the Church.
Commons describes it as 'crypto-Christian': its imagery could be read by pagans as philosophical and bucolic and by Christians as Christ the Good Shepherd.
cur:catacombs-via-salaria-sarcophagus.notes: Whether the patrons were Christian is debated; the central shepherd is included here as a probable image of Christ the Good Shepherd.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: In the lower miniature of this page, the haloed Christ stands before a crowned ruler, held by an attendant, while a group of men at the right, beside a city building, bear witness against him. The verse above reads 'false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out cruelty'.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Beneath the caption 'Extendens caelum sicut pellem' — 'who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain' — the haloed Christ stands with arms spread wide, holding up a great billowing canopy of cloud. The image presents Christ as the Word through whom the world was made.

cur:monumental-el-nazar-ascension.summary: In the vault of this small rock-cut church, Christ sits within a circular glory, raising his right hand in blessing, carried aloft by angels whose wings and haloes surround the medallion; below, further figures look upward. The bright blues, reds and yellows have survived despite heavy damage, giving a vivid sense of how such churches were once entirely painted.
facts: El Nazar is one of the rock-cut churches of Göreme within the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Göreme National Park.
In Cappadocian churches the Ascension, with Christ carried in a glory by angels, was a favourite subject for vaults and domes.

links.label: UNESCO: Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia

cur:monumental-el-nazar-ascension.notes: The scene is identified here as the Ascension from its composition (Christ in a glory borne by angels); the Commons description only says 'fresco of the El Nazar rock church'. Date generally given as 10th century.

cur:objects-andrews-diptych.summary: Two ivory leaves, each divided into three scenes by acanthus borders, show six miracles of Christ: the Raising of Lazarus, the Wedding at Cana, the Healing of the Leper, the Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes, the Healing of the Blind Man and the Healing of the Paralytic. In every panel a youthful, beardless Christ stretches out his hand or staff in a gesture of power, set against carefully drawn brick walls and buildings. The diptych is a fine witness to how the Carolingian court looked back to Early Christian art to picture the Lord as healer and giver of life.
facts: The V&A notes that its date is highly controversial: once taken for Late Antique work, it is now generally attributed to the Carolingian Renaissance of the 9th century, and the leaves may have been re-carved from a Late Antique diptych.
Faint painted figures of two haloed saints survive on the backs, and a large keyhole was cut into one leaf when the diptych was later reused, probably as the doors of a tabernacle or reliquary.
It was formerly at Palermo and in the Currie collection, and was given to the museum by F. E. Andrews through the National Art Collections Fund.
